Complete Empirical Research Plan  

================================================================================  
1. Identification Strategy  
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------  
Primary design: County-by-year staggered Difference-in-Differences (DiD) with an event-study extension.  

What varies exogenously?  
• The first local availability of scientifically bred, pest- or climate-resistant varieties (seeds for wheat, corn, cotton; breeding stock for dairy cattle, hogs, etc.).  
• Historical evidence shows that arrival dates were driven by biological and institutional factors external to any one county’s underlying productivity—e.g.  
  – Path of the boll-weevil (cotton) or Hessian fly (wheat) invasions, which created an immediate demand for resistant cultivars.  
  – Timing of federally funded experiment stations under the Hatch Act (1887) and rail shipment of seed from those stations.  
  – Migration of Mennonite communities who carried “Turkey Red” winter wheat (1874+) to selected Great-Plains counties.  

Because these shocks reached different counties in different years, we can treat the first year in which a county had demonstrably viable resistant seed/breeding stock as the “treatment” date and compare yield changes in subsequently treated counties with those not yet treated.  

Why DiD is appropriate  
• We observe long panels (Agricultural Censuses 1840–1920, quinquennial/decennial) with outcome variables (yields per acre, milk per cow, litter size, etc.) both before and after treatment for every county.  
• Treatment timing is plausibly orthogonal to short-run local yield movements but highly predictive of biological innovation exposure.  
• A staggered DiD with two-way fixed effects, supplemented by the recent Callaway-Sant’Anna / Sun-Abraham estimator, allows unbiased ATT when adoption is staggered.  

Supplementary design (robustness): Instrumental Variables  
• Endogenous adoption (innovating counties might be unusually forward-looking).  
• Instrument: distance to nearest Land-Grant experiment station in the year prior to treatment and historical share of Mennonite settlers (for wheat), both predetermined and powerful predictors of early variety arrival.  
• 2SLS on adop­tion share yields causal local average treatment effects (LATE) that complement the DiD estimates.  

================================================================================  
2. Treatment and Control  
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------  
Treatment variable  
Treatedct = 1 in county c, census year t, if by year t the county possessed (and was advertising in local farm papers) a pest/climate-resistant, scientifically bred variety i that matches the main local crop/livestock category (wheat, cotton, dairy cattle, hogs, etc.). Zero otherwise.  

Treatment timing  
FirstTreatc = first census year in which advertisements, extension bulletins or USDA Seed and Plant Introduction ledgers list the improved variety as locally available. After FirstTreatc, T stays at 1.  

Control group  
Counties that have not yet received the relevant resistant variety in the same year serve as contemporaneous controls. Eventually treated units provide the counterfactual paths for earlier adopters.  

Outcome variables  
lnYieldct = log yield per acre (crops) or log output per head (livestock).  

================================================================================  
3. Key Identifying Assumptions  
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------  
A1. Parallel trends (in absence of treatment, treated and not-yet-treated counties would have followed the same average yield trajectory).  
• Plausible? Pest shocks hit broad regions simultaneously, but experiment-station diffusion followed rail lines rather than differential underlying productivity. Pre-trend tests and visual event-study plots will assess it.  

A2. No anticipation. Farmers could not substantially raise yields in the years immediately before the new variety actually arrived.  
• Plausible? Adoption required physical seed or breeding stock; anticipation without seed stock is unlikely.  

A3. Stable Unit Treatment Value (no spillovers).  
• Plausible? Cross-county pollen drift and livestock sales could create spillovers. We will cluster by agro-climatic zones and test for border-spillovers; main estimates rely on the first 1–2 census rounds post treatment before large spillovers occur.  

A4. Exogenous timing conditional on controls.  
• Plausible? Experiment-station shipments were scheduled by scientists, not by local short-run yield shocks. We control for county fixed effects, state-by-year weather bins, and transportation access to meet this assumption.  

================================================================================  
4. Threats to Identification & Mitigation  
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------  
T1. Non-parallel pre-trends.  
• Address with flexible event-study (±4 census rounds), crop × region specific trends, and placebo treatment years.  

T2. Spillover diffusion (control counties adopt informally before official arrival).  
• Deal with (i) shrinking the control window to ≤10 years before adoption, (ii) spatial buffer—drop counties within 50 km of a treated neighbor, (iii) construct “treatment intensity” (share of acreage in improved seed) instead of 0/1.  

T3. Time-varying confounders: mechanization and rail access.  
• Add controls for density of reapers, tractors, and miles of rail per county-year from Historical Statistics; include county-specific linear time trends; use IV with distance-to-station to separate biological from mechanical innovation.  

================================================================================  
5. R Code Outline  
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------  
```r
# ---------------------------------------------------------------
# 0. Packages
library(data.table)
library(fixest)          # fast high-dimensional FE
library(did)             # Callaway-Sant’Anna DID
library(ivreg)           # IV estimation
# ---------------------------------------------------------------
# 1. Load data
census   <- fread("county_census_1840_1920.csv")   # yields, acreage, livestock
varDates <- fread("variety_arrival_by_county.csv") # FirstTreat year per county
stations <- fread("lg_station_distance.csv")       # Distance to station (km)
mennonite<- fread("mennonite_share_1880.csv")      # exogenous settler shares
# Merge
df <- census[varDates, on = .(county_fips)]
df <- df[stations,  on = .(county_fips)]
df <- df[mennonite,on = .(county_fips)]
# ---------------------------------------------------------------
# 2. Variable construction
df[, treated := as.integer(year >= FirstTreat)]
df[, ever_treated := !is.na(FirstTreat)]
df[, post_years := year - FirstTreat]              # for event study
df[, ln_yield := log(yield_per_acre)]
# IV
df[, Z1 := 1/dist_to_station]                      # proximity instrument
df[, Z2 := mennonite_share]                        # instrument for wheat
# ---------------------------------------------------------------
# 3. Main two-way FE DiD using Sun & Abraham
att_sa <- att_gt(yname = "ln_yield",
                 gname = "FirstTreat",
                 idname = "county_fips",
                 tname = "year",
                 xformla = ~ rail_miles + reaper_density,
                 data = df)

sa_event <- aggte(att_sa, type = "dynamic", min_e = -4, max_e = 6)
summary(sa_event)     # Pre-trend & dynamic effects plot
# ---------------------------------------------------------------
# 4. Simple 2-way FE (for comparison)
model_fe <- feols(ln_yield ~ treated + rail_miles + reaper_density |
                  county_fips + year, cluster = ~state_fips, data = df)
etable(model_fe)
# ---------------------------------------------------------------
# 5. IV robustness (2SLS)
// adoptrate = share of acreage in improved seed
iv_mod <- ivreg(ln_yield ~ adoptrate + rail_miles + reaper_density |
                          Z1 + Z2 + rail_miles + reaper_density,
                data = df)
summary(iv_mod, diagnostics = TRUE)
# ---------------------------------------------------------------
# 6. Placebo check: shift treatment year +20
df[, placeboTreat := as.integer(year >= (FirstTreat + 20))]
placebo <- feols(ln_yield ~ placeboTreat | county_fips + year,
                 cluster = ~state_fips, data = df)
summary(placebo)
```  

================================================================================  
6. Expected Results  
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------  
Economic priors: Resistant, better-adapted varieties raise yields 5–10 percent in the first decade after arrival (0.05–0.10 log points), roughly one-half to two-thirds of the mechanical yield gains credited to early binders/reapers in the same era. Effects should be largest for wheat in the Great Plains (Turkey Red) and for cotton in boll-weevil-hit counties post 1892.  

================================================================================  
7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (staggered DiD)  
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------  
C1: No differential pre-trends ............ 0.8  
C2: No anticipation ........................ 0.9  
C3: No spillovers / SUTVA ................. 0.6  
C4: Exogenous timing of treatment ......... 0.7  
C5: Stable measurement of outcome ......... 0.9  
Average (out of 1) ........................ 0.78  

================================================================================  
This empirical plan marries rich historical data with modern causal inference tools, allowing a direct comparison of the productivity contribution of biological innovation relative to mechanization while honoring the institutional nuances of 19th-century American agriculture.
